content: Professional courtesy refers to the longstanding tradition among physicians of not charging one another for the medical treatment of their respective family members. This practice was originally intended to discourage physicians from treating their own family members as patients, thereby avoiding potential ethical conflicts, and to promote camaraderie and mutual respect within the medical community. The origins of this custom can be traced back to the time of Hippocrates. The term professional courtesy can also extend beyond the medical field to describe specific behaviors in other professions. For example, police officers may refrain from issuing traffic tickets to fellow officers, or lawyers may adhere to ethical standards of conduct when interacting with one another. In such cases, the phrase is applied in a literal or ethical sense to describe expected professional behavior. Within the medical profession, this tradition is still observed in countries such as the United States and Egypt. However, certain prominent physicians may choose to disregard this practice, often as a way to encourage their colleagues to seek care from other, less expensive providers. This deviation from the tradition may be motivated by a desire to reduce costs for fellow physicians or their families while still ensuring access to quality care.
